reason: PO leaf sheath auricle fits the grass blades and culm sheaths that are most of the examples. Petal and leaf-base auricles have no PO class. For those, 'exauriculate' already maps to not auriculate (R0625), so this rule should not reach them.

Speckled = spotted (C334). 'Pale' is the colour of the spots, a detail of the spots that can be stated about them. This follows linear-foveolate and the tinged colours, where the main quality is kept and the modifier is dropped.
Same as muticous/awnless/unawned (C348, R1196) on grass parts. On leaf apices, achenes or sepals, mutique means without a mucro or point, not without an awn.

Sarmentous is the French 'sarmenteux', meaning long flexible stems that lean on or scramble through other plants. It is reviewed as climbing for sarmentose (R0155, with this same part constraint) and for sarmenteux (R1460). Use the same parts for consistency.

Foveate (pitted) is the quality. The long shape of the pits is a detail of the pits and does not need its own class. Modifiers like this are dropped the same way elsewhere, for example 'longitudinally fissured' becomes fissured.

FLOPO_0991298 petiole-like is defined as a leaf blade base narrowed into a stalk resembling a petiole, and it has 'pseudopetiolate' as a synonym. That is exactly 'falsely petiolate'. Tapered loses the stalk-like base.

Geocarpic fruits ripen below the ground surface, which is FLOPO subterranean on the fruit. On the whole plant or a peduncle it describes a behaviour, not being underground. Seeds are covered through the fruit.

The examples are walls of moss leaf cells with no pores, meaning holes through the wall. PO has no class for a cell-wall pore, so 'pore absent' cannot be stated. 'Not perforate' (no holes) is the closest negation that exists.

'Sans limbe' on leaves, sheaths and cataphylls means without a blade, as in the reviewed 'bladeless' rule. For a calyx or corolla, the limb is the spreading upper part (calyx limb FLOPO_0986093, perianth limb FLOPO_0986104), not a leaf lamina.

This means a margin fringed with long soft hairs, so ciliated is the quality and is correct. 'Villoso-' only names the kind of hair. Villous (FLOPO_0991051) can be added as a second value, but the mapping as it stands is not wrong.
Anastomosing (branches rejoining into a network) fits interconnected veins and fern rhizomes. Elsewhere, for example connate parts or connected cells, it only means joined.

PATO sparse (PATO_0001609) is defined as 'scattered; spread irregularly, and at a distance from each other', which is exactly this phrase. This is the same as the reviewed 'sparsely scattered' (R1595) and 'sparsely distributed' (R1873).

This follows 'staminate' (C233) and the reviewed bearer rules R3370-R3372: PO staminate flower allows a gynoecium that aborted during development. 'Functionally' only notes that the female parts are rudimentary.

Pilose is the quality. 'Scattered' or 'sparsely' is a word of degree kept in the record. This is the same as 'sparsely pubescent' (R0080) and 'sparsely hirsute' (R1502). FLOPO pilose is itself defined with scattered hairs.

In the quality field, 'dehiscence (along a suture / transversale)' says the part opens, which is dehiscent. This matches 'dehiscing' (R0096). Indehiscent and more specific ways of opening have their own rules.
PO secondary leaf vein is a vein of a leaf. On lemmas, glumes, petals or bracts, lateral veins are not leaf veins and need a different anatomy class.

'Increasing' on its own is a general word: increasing in size, number or diameter, or a change along the part. Accrescent applies only when the text names it or says the part enlarges after flowering, and those cases have their own rules.
Density is the quality of the covering. What does the covering (hairs, scales) is a separate statement, as the previous review held for 'covered'.

Tooth-shaped (dentiform) is about how a part looks, not a fixed outline. Teeth can be narrow, hooked or rounded, so triangular claims too much. There is no dentiform class in PATO or FLOPO, and with only 7 statements a new term is not worth adding.
Quadrate moss leaf cells are square. 'Irregularly' only loosens the value, as an approximate value under pattern 01, the same way 'tinged' and '-ish' are handled.
A pseudo-axillary inflorescence (for example in Solanaceae) truly arises outside the axil and only looks axillary. That is what FLOPO extra-axillary states. No closer term exists.

In 'hairs glandular-tipped' the bearer is the hair, which has a gland at its tip. Handle it like the reviewed 'gland-tipped' rule (R0010): gland present at the apex. Glandular-pubescent describes a surface clothed with such hairs and is wrong on the hair itself. Stipitate-glandular has the same problem.
The key leaves out where the vein ends. 'Midvein extending' can continue 'to the apex' (percurrent), 'beyond the apex' (excurrent, FLOPO_0991162) or 'to the middle'. Map the full phrases instead.

Glossaries define obcuneate/obcuneiform as wedge-shaped with the narrow end at the apex, the reverse of cuneate. Floras use it loosely, so the word is ambiguous. With 5 statements, reject rather than force cuneate.
The previous review mapped geniculate to PATO bent (C191), and neither PATO nor FLOPO has a geniculate class. Its negation is therefore 'not bent', the same form as other negated values.

This is the same as the reviewed 'purple tinged' (R0666), 'tinged brown' (R0991) and 'tinged reddish' (R1639): the colour is purple, and 'tinged' is a qualifier meaning 'approximately' under pattern 01.
'Clearly defined' veinlets and alar regions are clearly visible, the same reading as 'distinct' (C176) and 'well-defined' (R0160). 'Ill-defined' already maps to inconspicuous (R0594).

Moss alar cells or a central strand that are not clearly differentiated do not stand out from the cells around them. This is the same reading as 'ill-defined' and 'indistinct', which map to inconspicuous (R0594). PATO 'undifferentiated' is about cell maturity and does not fit.

The examples are bracts whose base does not wrap round the axis. PO has a sheath class only for leaves, and the bare word 'sheath' was rejected as a generic part. So negating FLOPO sheathing is the best grounded reading for bracts. Leaf cases are covered by 'sheathless' (R0461).

'Stems defoliate proximally' says the leaves are absent from the lower stem now. Where to put it on the stem comes from the part-of-bearer pattern, and words of time ('at flowering') come from context words. This is the same as 'aphyllous' (R0373).
